questions.q: Why does this workflow install dbt-snowflake instead of dbt-postgres, the adapter used in the original Git/CI-CD course's version of this pattern?
options: dbt-snowflake is a newer, generally better-performing package in every case
This platform's warehouse is Snowflake, not Postgres, so the Snowflake-specific adapter is required to connect to it
dbt-postgres has been fully discontinued and no longer installs
There is no real difference between the two adapters
questions.explain: The adapter has to match the actual database platform — Snowflake here, versus Postgres in the original retail-orders-analytics example.

questions.q: Why can't the workflow rely on a developer's existing ~/.dbt/profiles.yml file?
options: GitHub Actions automatically deletes all YAML files before a run
A fresh GitHub Actions runner has no home directory full of personal config files and no real password sitting on disk — the file has to be generated at CI time
profiles.yml is not a supported file format in CI
dbt does not require a profiles.yml file when running in CI
questions.explain: Each CI run starts from a clean, disposable runner with none of a developer's local configuration — the workflow must create profiles.yml itself every time.

questions.q: Where do the real Snowflake connection values in the generated profiles.yml actually come from at run time?
options: They're hardcoded directly as literal text in the workflow YAML file
env_var(...) inside profiles.yml, fed by step-level env: reading from ${{ secrets.* }} — never written as literal text anywhere in the repo
They're read from a .env file committed to the repository
dbt generates random placeholder values automatically
questions.explain: The env_var()/secrets.* chain keeps every sensitive value out of the repo entirely, generated fresh from GitHub's encrypted secrets each run.

questions.q: Why does this workflow's dbt build step target schema: ci rather than dev or prod?
options: ci is just an alias for prod with a different name
CI builds into its own disposable schema with a narrowly-scoped credential, so a misbehaving CI run can't touch real production data
dbt requires every CI run to use a schema literally named ci
schema: ci is required so Snowflake can bill CI usage separately
questions.explain: A fourth, separate schema plus a scoped SNOWFLAKE_CI_USER credential is the least-privilege pattern — CI never has the access to reach dev or prod.

questions.q: Why does this step run dbt build rather than dbt run followed by a separate dbt test?
options: dbt build runs models and tests together in dependency order, so CI never builds a downstream model on top of data that just failed a test in the same run
dbt run and dbt test are deprecated commands that no longer exist
dbt build is required specifically inside GitHub Actions and nowhere else
There is no difference in outcome between the two approaches
questions.explain: This reuses Chapter 4 and 15's exact reasoning: dbt build stops a bad test result from letting dependent models build on top of it, within the same run.
